name: Scattering and absorption in climate
summary: Rayleigh and Mie scattering and molecular absorption set atmospheric radiative transfer, aerosol forcing, cloud albedo and the greenhouse effect.

name: Cherenkov timing in PET
summary: Prompt Cherenkov photons from 511 keV photoelectrons in crystals such as BGO are exploited for sub-100 ps time-of-flight PET timing.

name: Cherenkov light in radiotherapy
summary: Cherenkov emission from therapy beams in tissue is used for dose imaging and verification; it is also a nuisance in fibre dosimeters.

name: Accelerator radiation losses and damping
summary: Synchrotron radiation loss limits ring energy and, via radiation reaction, provides damping and quantum excitation that set equilibrium emittance.

name: Light-source design from radiation formulas
summary: Source brightness and spectra are designed using the classical radiation formulas, with coherent enhancement when bunch length falls below the wavelength.

name: Liénard–Wiechert to undulator radiation
summary: Bending-magnet and undulator spectra, critical energy and relativistic beaming derive directly from Larmor/Liénard radiation, with $\gamma$-boosted forward cones.

name: Raman scattering as inelastic light scattering
summary: Raman spectroscopy is inelastic scattering from polarizability modulation by molecular vibrations, extending Rayleigh scattering from an induced dipole.

name: Aerosol and cloud scattering in forcing
summary: Aerosol direct and cloud albedo effects are Mie scattering with size-dependent efficiency; the sky's blue and clouds' white arise from the same Rayleigh-to-Mie crossover.

name: Compton and Rayleigh scattering in X-ray imaging
summary: Compton and Rayleigh scattering govern X-ray attenuation, scatter degradation of radiographs and CT contrast, and dose deposition.

name: Light scattering in tissue and diffuse optics
summary: Tissue optics relies on Mie/Rayleigh scattering and the diffusion approximation to radiative transfer to image and measure oxygenation in turbid media.

name: Thermodynamic limits of energy devices
summary: Thermoelectrics, solar cells and batteries are bounded by second-law efficiency limits; ZT maps to a fraction of Carnot efficiency, and finite-time engine analysis applies.

name: Carnot bounds on solar cell efficiency
summary: Solar cells act as heat engines between the Sun and ambient temperature; the Shockley–Queisser limit and Landsberg/Carnot bounds follow from entropy generation in photon absorption and emission.
breaks: Photovoltaic conversion is quantum and band-gap limited, not a cyclic engine.

name: Photovoltaics as thermodynamic converters
summary: Detailed balance between absorbed and emitted blackbody radiation sets the SQ limit; thermodynamic treatments give ultimate limits for multijunction and hot-carrier cells.

name: Adsorption isotherms and chemical potential
summary: Langmuir and BET isotherms follow from equating the chemical potential of adsorbed and gas phases, i.e. a lattice-gas grand canonical calculation.

name: Electrochemical potential and battery voltage
summary: Cell voltage equals the Gibbs free-energy change per charge, with the open-circuit voltage from the chemical potential difference of lithium in the two electrodes.

name: Network science of biological regulation and spreading
summary: Scale-free and small-world network structure describes gene regulation, metabolic and neural networks, and epidemic spreading with vanishing thresholds.

name: Coherent backscattering and weak localization of waves
summary: Weak localization of light in turbid media produces coherent backscattering enhancement, which modifies diffuse optics and speckle statistics in tissue.
breaks: Strong localization is not reached in tissue; transport is nearly classical diffusion.

name: Percolation in composite electrodes and electrolytes
summary: Ionic and electronic conduction in composite battery electrodes and solid electrolytes depends on percolating pathways with critical thresholds and power-law conductivity.

name: Protein folding funnels and spin-glass landscapes
summary: Random-energy-model ideas and the principle of minimal frustration describe folding landscapes; glass transition temperature and funnel gap separate foldable sequences from glassy ones.
breaks: Evolved proteins are strongly non-random and minimally frustrated, unlike true spin glasses.

name: Statistical physics of neural computation
summary: Hopfield-network and replica methods from spin glasses are used to model neural memory, capacity and learning in neural biophysics.

name: Learning theory and protein structure inference
summary: Spin-glass landscape concepts and Boltzmann-machine/Potts inference (direct coupling analysis) link learning theory to protein folding and structure prediction.

name: Partition functions in transition-state theory
summary: Eyring transition-state theory writes rate constants as ratios of partition functions, and equilibrium constants follow from molecular partition functions.

name: Information-theoretic limits of quantum metrology
summary: Fisher information and Cramér–Rao bounds set measurement precision, mirroring maximum-entropy and information-geometry formulations of statistical mechanics.
breaks: Quantum Fisher information involves non-commuting observables with no classical-entropy counterpart.

name: Information limits in living systems
summary: Sensing precision, kinetic proofreading and gene regulation are bounded by mutual information and Landauer-type energy costs, using Shannon entropy and maximum entropy models.

name: Maximum entropy and information in image reconstruction
summary: Maximum-entropy priors and Shannon information underlie regularised image reconstruction and noise-limited image quality in CT and MRI.

name: Planck law and Earth's radiative balance
summary: Planck's blackbody spectrum and Stefan–Boltzmann law fix Earth's emission temperature; greenhouse absorption modifies the outgoing spectrum band by band.

name: Poisson counting statistics in emission imaging
summary: Radioactive decay counts are Poisson fluctuations, so SPECT and PET image noise scales as 1/√N, which governs time-of-flight gains.

name: Active and driven matter in living systems
summary: Exclusion processes, KPZ growth and active-matter nonequilibrium steady states model molecular traffic, tissue growth, bacterial colonies and collective cell motion.

name: Self-organized criticality in earthquakes
summary: Gutenberg–Richter power-law earthquake statistics and stick-slip fault models such as Burridge–Knopf and OFC are the standard examples of self-organized criticality and avalanche dynamics.
breaks: Real faults show characteristic-earthquake and aftershock correlations not captured by simple SOC models.

name: Vlasov-Boltzmann kinetics of charged beams
summary: Beam distributions evolve by Vlasov/Fokker–Planck equations in phase space, as in collisionless kinetic theory; Liouville's theorem underlies emittance conservation and cooling is a Fokker–Planck process.
breaks: Beams are far from equilibrium, with long-range space-charge and no collision-driven thermalization.

name: From Boltzmann kinetics to atmospheric fluid equations
summary: Chapman–Enskog reduction of the Boltzmann equation gives the Navier–Stokes transport coefficients used in atmospheric models; mean free path sets the continuum validity.

name: Onsager reciprocity and thermoelectric transport
summary: Seebeck and Peltier coefficients are related by Onsager reciprocity (Kelvin relation), and ZT follows from the matrix of transport coefficients constrained by the second law.

name: Fluctuation-dissipation limits on sensor noise
summary: Thermal noise in SQUIDs, resonators and magnetometers is tied to dissipation by the fluctuation–dissipation theorem (Johnson–Nyquist), setting sensitivity floors.

name: Langevin dynamics of tethered molecules
summary: Optical-tweezer bead and molecule dynamics are overdamped Langevin processes; force spectroscopy, Kramers escape and diffusion analyses use Fokker–Planck theory.

name: Kramers rate theory and reaction rates
summary: Barrier-crossing rates in solution follow Kramers theory, interpolating between transition-state theory and diffusion-limited regimes with friction.
breaks: Kramers theory assumes a single reaction coordinate with Markovian friction.

name: Hasselmann stochastic climate model
summary: Slow climate variability is modelled as an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process, with fast weather as noise forcing the slow ocean and ice variables.
breaks: Weather noise is not strictly white and the system lacks detailed balance.

name: Diffusion and speckle in diffuse optics
summary: Photon transport in tissue reduces to a diffusion equation from random walks; diffusing-wave spectroscopy and Doppler/speckle techniques probe Brownian motion and blood flow.

name: Biophysics as stochastic thermodynamics
summary: Cellular sensing, motors and information processing are analysed by entropy production and thermodynamic uncertainty relations, linking precision to dissipation.

name: Fluctuation theorems for molecular machines
summary: Molecular motors and folding transitions operate far from equilibrium at kT scale; entropy production and Jarzynski/Crooks relations quantify their dissipation and free energies.

name: Dissipation cost of kinetic proofreading and sensing
summary: Energy dissipation buys accuracy in proofreading and sensing; entropy production bounds error rates and information rates.

name: Pulling experiments verify Jarzynski and Crooks
summary: Optical-tweezer unfolding of RNA hairpins verified Jarzynski and Crooks relations, recovering equilibrium free energies from nonequilibrium work distributions.

name: Lattice-gas models of adsorbate ordering
summary: Adsorbed monolayers map onto Ising lattice gases, with ordering transitions and surface reconstructions in Ising, Potts and universality classes; kinetic Monte Carlo models catalytic kinetics.

name: Tipping points and bifurcations in climate
summary: Ice-albedo and AMOC bistability resemble Landau free-energy double wells with first-order jumps and hysteresis, and critical slowing down serves as an early-warning signal.
breaks: Climate is driven and dissipative with no free energy to minimise.

name: Polymer scaling and coarse-graining of biomolecules
summary: Renormalization-group scaling gives polymer exponents for unfolded chains, and coarse-grained models of proteins use the same logic of eliminating fast degrees of freedom.

name: Fluctuating membranes and 2D defect physics
summary: Two-dimensional membranes and the hexatic/crystalline phases share 2D melting and defect-unbinding physics, plus thermal-undulation renormalisation of bending rigidity.
breaks: Membranes have out-of-plane fluctuations and fluid lipid order, so BKT applies only to in-plane ordered layers.

name: Phase-space cooling in beams and atoms
summary: Stochastic, electron and laser cooling of stored ion beams parallel atomic laser cooling: both shrink phase-space volume via dissipative coupling, with laser-cooled ion beams bridging them.
breaks: Liouville's theorem forbids cooling with conservative forces alone; accelerator beams are classical and macroscopically charged.

name: Atomic sensors and clocks
summary: Atom interferometers, optical clocks and atomic magnetometers share Ramsey interrogation of coherent atomic superpositions, limited by projection noise and coherence time.

name: Quantum gravimetry for geophysics
summary: Atom-interferometric gravimeters and clock-based relativistic geodesy measure gravity potential differences, applied to Earth-interior mass changes and hydrology.

name: Chemical physics rests on atomic structure
summary: Atomic level structure, fine/hyperfine coupling and spectroscopy provide the foundation for chemical physics, from orbitals to spectroscopic probes of molecules.

name: Atomic to molecular spectroscopy
summary: Selection rules, term structure and spectroscopic techniques from atoms extend to molecular rotational, vibrational and electronic spectra, adding nuclear motion via Born–Oppenheimer separation.

name: Spectroscopy shared toolkit
summary: Laser spectroscopy techniques, line-shape analysis and selection rules developed for atoms are used on molecules, and ultrafast molecular methods feed back into AMO.

name: Optical trapping: atoms to biomolecules
summary: Gradient-force optical traps developed for cooling and trapping atoms became optical tweezers that manipulate single biomolecules and measure piconewton forces.

name: Tweezers return: biophysics to atoms
summary: Optical tweezer technology links single-molecule force spectroscopy and neutral-atom tweezer arrays; the same focused-beam dipole trap physics underlies both.

name: Cold-atom simulation of chemical models
summary: Programmable atomic lattices emulate Hubbard and spin-boson-type models relevant to electron transfer and correlated electrons, offering analog simulation of chemical physics Hamiltonians.

name: Chemical physics and ultracold molecules
summary: Molecular structure, potential surfaces and collision theory from chemical physics underpin cooling and control of molecules and controlled ultracold reactions.

name: Molecular spectroscopy for EDM and cooling
summary: Rovibrational structure and Franck–Condon factors determine which molecules can be laser-cooled, and precision molecular spectroscopy underlies electron-EDM searches.

name: Ultracold chemistry and reaction dynamics
summary: Ultracold molecular collisions probe reactions at the quantum threshold, where single partial waves, resonances and tunnelling dominate over thermal averaging, testing potential energy surfaces.

name: Decoherence limits sensors
summary: Environmental decoherence sets T2 and thus sensitivity of NV, atomic and SQUID sensors, while sensors also serve as probes of environmental noise spectra; entangled probes are more fragile.

name: Quantum biology and open dynamics
summary: Exciton transport in photosynthetic complexes is modelled with open-system master equations, where noise may assist transfer; relevance of coherence is debated.
breaks: Long-lived coherence claims were contested; biological functional relevance remains unclear.

name: Open-system dynamics of molecules
summary: Redfield and Lindblad master equations model electron and energy transfer in solvents, connecting to Marcus theory and system-bath treatments of reaction dynamics.

name: Fluctuation theorems in single molecules
summary: Jarzynski and Crooks relations were verified by pulling single RNA molecules with optical tweezers and extended to quantum systems in trapped-ion experiments.

name: Entanglement and quantum Fisher information
summary: Metrological gain requires entanglement: the quantum Fisher information exceeding N bounds sensitivity and witnesses multipartite entanglement.

name: NV centres: qubit and sensor
summary: The nitrogen-vacancy centre is both a spin qubit and the leading solid-state nanoscale magnetometer, using identical initialization, microwave control and optical readout.

name: Silicon spin qubits and transistors
summary: Quantum-dot spin qubits are implemented in MOSFET-like gate-defined structures, so semiconductor industrial processing and device physics transfer directly.

name: Quantum computing for electronic structure
summary: Phase estimation and variational eigensolvers target molecular ground-state energies, aiming to beat the exponential cost of exact classical full CI.

name: Quantum simulation of catalysts
summary: Strongly correlated active sites such as FeMoco in nitrogenase are prime targets for quantum simulation, where classical DFT struggles.

name: Kinetic proofreading and error suppression
summary: Both biology and fault-tolerant quantum computing suppress error rates by spending energy and repeating checks, reaching lower error through dissipative, multi-step discrimination.
breaks: Proofreading is classical and thermodynamic; QEC uses syndromes and non-demolition measurement.

name: Solid-state device fabrication
summary: Superconducting qubits rely on semiconductor lithography and thin-film fabrication, and cryogenic CMOS control electronics link both; spin qubits are built in silicon MOS devices.

name: MRI as spin dynamics
summary: MRI is nuclear spin-1/2 precession in a magnetic field: Larmor frequency, Bloch equations, RF pulses and relaxation follow directly from angular-momentum algebra.

name: Spin and positronium physics in PET
summary: Positron annihilation via para-positronium produces back-to-back 511 keV photons, with angular-momentum and parity selection rules fixing the two-photon signature used in PET.

name: Perturbation and variational theory in chemistry
summary: Hartree–Fock, Møller–Plesset and configuration interaction are direct applications of the variational principle and Rayleigh–Schrödinger perturbation theory to many-electron systems.

name: Quantum chemistry as applied approximation theory
summary: Basis-set expansions, perturbative corrections and variational optimization in quantum chemistry are the approximation methods of core quantum mechanics at scale.

name: Adiabatic theorem and Born–Oppenheimer
summary: The Born–Oppenheimer approximation is the adiabatic theorem applied to fast electrons; its breakdown near avoided crossings gives Landau–Zener transitions and nonadiabatic reaction dynamics.

name: Surface science and solvable models
summary: Tunnelling through barriers underlies scanning tunnelling microscopy, and square-well and Morse-type solvable models describe adsorbate binding and vibrations.

name: Berry phase at conical intersections
summary: Conical intersections between potential energy surfaces carry a Berry phase of π, which changes nuclear wavefunction boundary conditions and affects reaction outcomes.

name: Instantons and tunnelling rates
summary: Semiclassical instanton theory computes tunnelling-dominated reaction rates and splittings, extending transition-state theory with Euclidean-action saddle points.

name: Optomechanical quantum-limited sensing
summary: Optomechanical force and displacement sensors operate at the standard quantum limit with squeezed-light backaction evasion, as in LIGO-type and accelerometer devices.

name: FEL light statistics and coherence
summary: SASE FEL radiation starts from shot noise and has chaotic-like spiky thermal statistics, characterised by g2 coherence functions, with seeded FELs approaching laser coherence.

name: Single-photon detection in PET and optics
summary: Photon counting with SiPMs, avalanche photodiodes and fast timing is shared between quantum optics and time-of-flight PET, as is Poisson counting statistics.

name: Photon counting in diffuse optics
summary: Time-correlated single-photon counting and SNSPDs enable diffuse optical tomography and fluorescence lifetime imaging in biomedical optics.

name: Applied devices exploit squeezed light
summary: Device-level sensing and metrology use nonclassical light from quantum optics to reduce shot noise below the standard quantum limit.

name: Squeezing and entanglement-enhanced sensing
summary: Squeezed and entangled probe states beat the standard quantum limit toward the Heisenberg limit, applied in interferometers, magnetometers and spin ensembles.

name: Synchrotron radiation: light sources and the M87* ring
summary: The EHT's 1.3 mm emission is synchrotron radiation from relativistic electrons gyrating in magnetic fields near the horizon, governed by the same critical-frequency and polarization physics that light sources are engineered around. EHT polarimetry reads the synchrotron polarization pattern to map the geometry of the magnetic field.
sources: Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration (2019). "First M87 Event Horizon Telescope Results. I. The Shadow of the Supermassive Black Hole". *Astrophys. J. Lett.* 875, L1. [arXiv:1906.11238](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.11238)

name: Fourier-plane imaging: VLBI u-v coverage and MRI k-space
summary: An interferometer measures Fourier components (visibilities) of the sky, and MRI measures k-space samples of the magnetization, so both reconstruct images from sparse Fourier data using regularized or compressed-sensing inversion. Bracewell's projection-slice reconstructions in radio astronomy anticipated the mathematics of CT.
map: V(u,v)=\iint I(x,y)e^{-2\pi i(ux+vy)}dx\,dy\ \leftrightarrow\ S(\mathbf k)=\int m(\mathbf r)e^{-2\pi i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf r}d\mathbf r
breaks: VLBI lacks absolute phases and must rely on closure quantities, while MRI records complex k-space data directly.
sources: Lauterbur (1973). "Image Formation by Induced Local Interactions: Examples Employing Nuclear Magnetic Resonance". *Nature* 242, 190. [doi:10.1038/242190a0](https://doi.org/10.1038/242190a0)

Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration (2019). "First M87 Event Horizon Telescope Results. I. The Shadow of the Supermassive Black Hole". *Astrophys. J. Lett.* 875, L1. [arXiv:1906.11238](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.11238)

name: Wave blocking on currents as a white-hole horizon
summary: Surface waves travelling against a strengthening current stop where the current speed equals their group velocity, which in the acoustic-metric picture is a white-hole horizon. Water-tank experiments measured Hawking-like mode conversion with a thermal-like amplitude ratio, and wave blocking at tidal inlets and river mouths is the same effect in the ocean.
breaks: Water waves are strongly dispersive (no exact horizon or Lorentz symmetry) and damped by viscosity, and the experiments probe classical stimulated conversion; the spontaneous quantum emission is far too cold to measure.
sources: Hawking (1975). "Particle creation by black holes". *Commun. Math. Phys.* 43, 199. [doi:10.1007/BF02345020](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02345020)

name: Photon sphere and transition state as unstable bottlenecks
summary: The photon sphere is a normally hyperbolic invariant set of unstable orbits that separates capture from escape, like the dividing surface of transition-state theory in reaction dynamics. Its Lyapunov exponent sets the damping of eikonal quasinormal modes in the same way that the curvature of the barrier top sets the imaginary parts of quantized transition-state resonances.
breaks: The black-hole case is a single geodesic or linear wave on a fixed background, with no thermal ensemble or energy redistribution; reaction transition states live in many-dimensional phase space with recrossing and intramolecular energy flow.

name: Atom interferometry hunts screened fifth forces
summary: Chameleon and symmetron screening hide a scalar fifth force inside dense bodies behind a thin shell, but individual atoms in an ultra-high-vacuum chamber are unscreened. Atom-interferometric acceleration measurements near a source mass have therefore excluded much of the chameleon parameter space proposed to explain dark energy.

name: Junk radiation and geostrophic adjustment
summary: Both fields evolve hyperbolic equations from initial data that must satisfy elliptic conditions: the Einstein constraints, or geostrophic and nonlinear-normal-mode balance. Data that are off the physical slow manifold shed spurious fast waves (junk radiation in binary simulations, inertia–gravity waves in weather models) that must be discarded before results are trusted, and both fields use Berger–Oliger adaptive mesh refinement.
breaks: The Einstein constraints are exact identities that the evolution preserves, whereas atmospheric balance is approximate (small Rossby number) and not conserved; junk radiation leaves through the outer boundary, while unbalanced gravity waves can persist and are actively filtered.

name: Clocks and atom interferometers test redshift and the EP
summary: Pound and Rebka first measured gravitational redshift over 22.5 m; optical lattice clocks now resolve it across millimetres. Atom interferometers comparing two isotopes test the weak equivalence principle near 1e-12, and these are the same quantum devices used as gravimeters and timing references.
sources: Pound & Rebka (1960). "Apparent Weight of Photons". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 4, 337. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.4.337](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.4.337)

name: Frame dragging read out by SQUIDs and Sagnac gyroscopes
summary: Gravity Probe B measured geodetic and frame-dragging precession by reading the London moment of spinning superconducting rotors with SQUID magnetometers. Ring-laser and atom-interferometric Sagnac gyroscopes, which are also quantum-sensing devices, have been proposed to detect the Lense–Thirring effect on the ground (GINGER).
sources: Everitt et al. (2011). "Gravity Probe B: Final Results of a Space Experiment to Test General Relativity". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 106, 221101. [arXiv:1105.3456](https://arxiv.org/abs/1105.3456)

name: Relativistic geodesy: clocks measure the geopotential
summary: A clock's rate depends on the gravitational potential, so comparing optical clocks at the 1e-18 level resolves height differences of about 1 cm, turning a GR test into a geodetic probe of Earth's gravity field and mass redistribution. In the other direction, satellite tests of frame dragging (LAGEOS) are limited by how well Earth's mass distribution is modelled.
sources: Hafele & Keating (1972). "Around-the-World Atomic Clocks: Predicted Relativistic Time Gains". *Science* 177, 166. [doi:10.1126/science.177.4044.166](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.177.4044.166)

name: Earth's normal modes as a gravitational-wave antenna
summary: A GW's tidal acceleration drives the quadrupolar modes of an elastic body, the principle of Weber's bar. Dyson (1969) computed Earth's seismic response to a GW, and records of Earth's free oscillations have been used to bound the stochastic GW background; lunar seismic antennas are now proposed for the decihertz band.

name: Squeezed light beats the shot-noise limit in LIGO
summary: LIGO is the largest quantum sensor: shot noise enters through the vacuum at the dark port, so injecting squeezed vacuum (now frequency-dependent) lowers it, the same squeezed-state toolkit used in atomic magnetometers and clocks. The trade-off between shot noise and radiation-pressure noise defines the standard quantum limit that all continuous displacement sensors share.
sources: Caves (1981). "Quantum-mechanical noise in an interferometer". *Phys. Rev. D* 23, 1693. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevD.23.1693](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevD.23.1693)
Degen, Reinhard & Cappellaro (2017). "Quantum sensing". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 89, 035002. [arXiv:1611.02427](https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.02427)

name: Laser-read oscillators in a thermal bath
summary: LIGO's test-mass suspensions and an optically trapped bead are both harmonic oscillators in a thermal bath, read out with light, whose displacement noise is fixed by the fluctuation–dissipation theorem. Optical tweezers are calibrated from the Lorentzian Brownian spectrum, and LIGO's thermal-noise budget comes from the mechanical loss entering the same formula.
breaks: LIGO works far above resonance, with tiny structural loss angles and quantum back-action, while a trapped bead is overdamped in water, classical, and probes forces rather than strain.

name: Ocean microseism as a GW-detector noise source
summary: Opposing ocean swells generate pressure fluctuations at twice the wave frequency (the Longuet-Higgins mechanism), which travel through the ground as the 0.1–0.3 Hz secondary microseism. This ground motion dominates the seismic input to LIGO and Virgo and causes lock losses during ocean storms, so it shapes their isolation and control design.

name: Newtonian noise and prompt elastogravity signals
summary: Seismic waves compress rock and so change local gravity. In GW detectors this Newtonian noise cannot be shielded and limits sensitivity below about 10 Hz, which is why the Einstein Telescope will be underground and why seismometer arrays are used for subtraction. In seismology the same effect produced prompt elastogravity signals, seen before the P-waves of the 2011 Tohoku earthquake.

name: SRF cavities as high-frequency GW detectors
summary: Superconducting RF cavities built for accelerators, with quality factors above 1e10, are being repurposed as heterodyne GW detectors. A passing high-frequency GW deforms the walls and couples to the field, pumping power between two nearly degenerate modes (the MAGO concept) and opening a kHz–GHz window beyond the reach of interferometers.

name: Atom interferometers: from gravimeters to GW detectors
summary: The light-pulse atom interferometry used in quantum gravimeters and gradiometers is being scaled up into long-baseline gravitational-wave detectors (MAGIS-100, AION) for the 0.1–10 Hz gap between LIGO and LISA. The GW signal is a differential phase between two atom clouds that share the same laser pulses, so the detector is a gradiometer read out like a clock.
sources: Degen, Reinhard & Cappellaro (2017). "Quantum sensing". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 89, 035002. [arXiv:1611.02427](https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.02427)

name: LISA-style laser ranging weighs the oceans (GRACE-FO)
summary: GRACE Follow-On carries a laser ranging interferometer that flight-tested the heterodyne inter-spacecraft ranging LISA will use. Its nanometre-precision ranging maps time-variable gravity, which measures ocean-bottom pressure, ice-sheet loss and the mass part of sea-level rise; combined with Argo floats it isolates ocean heat uptake.
sources: Amaro-Seoane et al. (2017). "Laser Interferometer Space Antenna". [arXiv:1702.00786](https://arxiv.org/abs/1702.00786)

name: Tensor networks: DMRG chemistry and MERA holography
summary: Matrix-product-state DMRG is a production quantum-chemistry method for strongly correlated active spaces. Its multiscale relative MERA builds a discrete AdS-like bulk whose minimal cuts give a Ryu–Takayanagi-like entanglement bound, and both methods work because ground-state entanglement obeys area laws.
breaks: Molecules lack the scale invariance that makes MERA holographic, and chemical DMRG orders orbitals on a 1D chain rather than building a geometric bulk.
sources: Ryu & Takayanagi (2006). "Holographic Derivation of Entanglement Entropy from AdS/CFT". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 96, 181602. [arXiv:hep-th/0603001](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/0603001)
